notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar and his huge allied army surrounded Jerusalem and the nearby cities of Judah. God sent Jeremiah to deliver a message during this terrifying siege. The Lord showed that Judah's enemies were not acting outside of His control.

God commanded Jeremiah to tell King Zedekiah that the city was doomed. The Lord Himself was handing Jerusalem over to the king of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar would conquer the city and burn it to the ground.

Zedekiah was warned that he would not escape the invaders. He would be captured and brought directly before the king of Babylon to speak with him face to face. After that meeting, he would be carried away into exile.
Even while announcing judgment, God offered Zedekiah a word of mercy. The king was told that he would not be executed or die by the sword in battle. God spared his life from immediate violence.

Zedekiah was promised a peaceful end by natural death while in captivity. When he died, his people would honor him with burning spices and mourn for him as they did for earlier kings. God gave His personal pledge that this would happen.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that Zedekiah remained a prisoner in Babylon until death, where the Jewish exiles were allowed to give him an honorable burial.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah faithfully delivered every part of this hard message to King Zedekiah in Jerusalem. Delivering bad news to a reigning king took great courage. Jeremiah put his duty to God above his own personal safety.

At that time, only Jerusalem and two other fortified towns were still holding out against Babylon. These last outposts were Lachish and Azekah, guarding the roads in southern Judah. All the other walled cities of Judah had already fallen.

A new message came to Jeremiah after King Zedekiah made an agreement with the people of Jerusalem. Under the pressure of the Babylonian siege, they decided to proclaim freedom for their Hebrew slaves. This covenant was made solemnly in God's temple.

The agreement required everyone to release all their fellow Israelites who were serving as male or female slaves. God's ancient law did not allow one Jew to hold another in lifelong servitude. They were supposed to treat their brothers as free people.
The rulers and all the slave owners initially agreed to the terms. They obeyed the king's order and released their servants. For a brief moment, it looked like true repentance and obedience to God.

Soon afterward, the slave owners changed their minds and broke their promise. When the Babylonian army temporarily pulled back, the owners forced the freed men and women back into slavery. Their sudden show of obedience vanished as soon as the danger seemed gone.
The Lord saw this dishonest behavior and sent Jeremiah to confront the people. God refused to let their treachery go unaddressed.

God reminded the people of the original covenant He made with their ancestors. He had rescued Israel from brutal slavery in Egypt. Because God had set them free, He expected them to treat their own people with mercy.
The law stated that any Hebrew who sold himself into service should go free in the seventh year, after serving six years. Yet Israel's ancestors had repeatedly ignored and disobeyed this command.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that the six years of service before freedom symbolize six thousand years of human history under Satan before being set free in Christ's millennial reign.

notes.meaning: God acknowledged that the people had recently done what was right by setting their neighbors free. They had even ratified this covenant before God inside His holy temple. That made their pledge especially sacred.

By taking their slaves back, the people dragged God's holy name through the mud. Breaking an oath sworn in His temple showed utter contempt for the Lord. They robbed their neighbors of the freedom they had just granted.

God answered their broken promise with grim justice. Since they refused to give real freedom to their brothers, God declared them free from His protection. They were now exposed to death by war, disease, and starvation, becoming an object of horror to the world.

God declared that He would cut the covenant-breakers apart just like the calf they had used in their ceremony. When making their vow, they had sliced a calf in two and walked between the halves. This ancient ritual was a way of saying, may God tear me to pieces like this animal if I break my word.

This judgment targeted everyone who took part in the ceremony, from the royal court and priests to the common citizens. No one was excused because of wealth or power. Every leader who walked between the pieces of the calf was held accountable.

God announced that He would surrender these dishonest leaders to enemies who wanted to kill them. They would receive no burial, and their corpses would be left for wild animals and birds to eat. This was seen as the most shameful end possible.

King Zedekiah and his royal officials would also be handed over to their deadly enemies. The Babylonian army had marched away for a brief time to fight off Egypt, but their departure was only temporary. God would not allow the leaders of Judah to escape.

God declared that He was the one ordering the Babylonian soldiers to return. They would besiege Jerusalem once more, capture it, and burn it to ashes. The surrounding towns of Judah would become an empty wasteland where no one lived.
